items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-06-06
items.q: Harold Holmes wrote the arrangements... we added Harold Holmes to the bass section.

ctx.x: You had a regular arranger for your band?

There was five fellas in the band that arranged at one time. Harold Holmes later on when Jimmy Johnson was getting a little slow, we added Harold Holmes to the bass section. We also had a tuba, so we had a tuba, two bass fiddles in the band at the same time. Harold Holmes wrote the arrangements, another terrific trumpet player that I picked up in the eastern states, Billy Douglas. He, unfortunately he was, oh he liked to hit the bottle too much we say. But he would have been one of the mighty, mighty greats for…
But I'm just agreeing that I do some of that myself.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: And of course we had Harold Holmes, who did a tremendous job of arranging. He was one of the bass players.

ctx.x: Tim came up with something about arrangements. Did you pay the men to do arrangements?

We didn't have any money to pay ourselves nothing. Would you have a bond for everybody in the band? Well, everybody in the band worked as a family. That's what it was. If we made ten dollars, we'd split ten dollars. By the same token, if we made a hundred, we'd split a hundred. And everybody wanted the band to be the best and everybody would chip in the things that they knew how. I think Cottrell made one or two arrangements. Herbert Hall made some. And of course we had Harold Holmes, who did a tremendous job of…

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1969-12-30
items.q: we had a great arranger in the person of Harold Holmes, who was a bass player. And he's now in Canada. He wrote some tremendous arrangements for the band.

ctx.x: Okay, this is Don Albert, Real 2, December the 30th, 1969, I believe it is. Okay, I wanted to ask you about the arrangers in your band a little bit. Now, who did most of the arrangers?

Well, when the band first left here, when I organized it here in New Orleans, there weren't any arrangers. We would take the stocks and we would rearrange the stocks to fit what we wanted, and how we wanted it. But we were concentrating on our original style of playing. And the first arranger that I had in the band was a fellow out of Little Rock, Arkansas. He is still living today. His name is Philander Tiller, an alto player. Now, Phil was a tremendous arranger. And he could write arrangements that he couldn't…
Did you ever hear him talk about Cuba? Cuban Bennett?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-12-30
items.q: And then later on I added Harold Holmes, who's now in Canada, who did most of my arranging.

ctx.x: So you got a real close song, didn't you?

That was the first bass song. And then when we went up a little further, when we added Geechee Robinson, another drum roll. We had Nick Turner, another bass record. I had Jimmy Johnson on the string bass. And I had Nick Turner on the Suze for MWM on the drum roll. And then later on I added Harold Holmes, who's now in Canada, who did most of my arranging. And as we traveled over the country, I added here, subtracted, added and subtracted.
And I found the change in the years. Did you ever play any other state fairs? You want to start it by now or is it?
